From Wiktionary, the free dictionary
See also: Nome, nomé, nõme, ñome, and -nôme

English

[edit]

Pronunciation

[edit]
  • (Received Pronunciation) IPA(key): /nəʊm/
  • Audio (Southern England):(file)
  • (General American) enPR: nōm, IPA(key): /noʊm/
  • Rhymes: -əʊm, -oʊm
  • Homophones: Nome, gnome

Etymology 1

[edit]

From French nome, from Ancient Greek νομός (nomós, “district”), from νέμω (némō, “to divide”). Doublet of nomos.

Noun

[edit]

nome (plural nomes)

  2. A prefecture or unit of regional government in Greece.
    Laconia is the southernmost nome in the Peloponnese.
  3. A territorial division of ancient Egypt.
    • 1983, Norman Mailer, Ancient Evenings:
      Yet the part will be as the whole, and you will be the High Priest in this nome of Egypt.
Derived terms
[edit]
  • nomarch
Translations
[edit]
prefecture in (modern) Greece
  • Esperanto: nomarĥio
  • Greek: νομός (el) m (nomós)
territorial division of ancient Egypt
  • Egyptian:

    (spꜣt f)
  • Esperanto: nomarĥio, nomarkio
  • Greek: νομός (el) m (nomós)
  • Polish: nom (pl) m
  • Portuguese: nomo (pt) m

Etymology 2

[edit]

From Ancient Greek νόμος (nómos), from νέμω (némō, “to divide”). Differs from Etymology 1 in the position of Ancient Greek accent, though from the same root.

Noun

[edit]

nome (plural nomes)

  2. A type of musical composition in Ancient Greece.
Translations
[edit]
type of musical composition in ancient Greece
  • Greek: νόμος (el) m (nómos)

Etymology 3

[edit]

Contraction.

Interjection

[edit]

nome

  2. (US, regional) Alternative form of no'm (“no ma'am”).
    • 1929, William Faulkner, The Sound and the Fury, Folio Society, published 2016, page 7:
      Mother said, “Is he cold, Versh.”
      “Nome.” Versh said.

Etymology 4

[edit]
English Wikipedia has an article on:
nome (mathematics)
Wikipedia

The sense "term" is from French -nôme, second element of binôme etc., again from Ancient Greek νομός (nomós) here in its sense "division". The name of the special function may be identical or may be an independent borrowing from the Greek.[1]

Noun

[edit]

nome

  2. (mathematics, obsolete) A term in an algebraic expression.
  3. (mathematics) A special function with which elliptic functions and modular forms can be described.

References

      Old Galician-Portuguese

      [edit]

      Etymology

      [edit]

      Inherited from Latin nōmen (“name”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁nómn̥.

      Pronunciation

      [edit]
      • IPA(key): /ˈnome/

      Noun

      [edit]

      nome m (plural nomes)

      1. name
        • a. 1284, Alfonso X of Castile, Cantigas de Santa Maria, Códice de los músicos, cantiga 111 (facsimile):
          […] Loado ſeia ſeu Nome.
          […] may his Name be praised.

      Portuguese

      [edit]

      Etymology

      [edit]

      From Old Galician-Portuguese nome, from Latin nōmen (“name”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁nómn̥.

      Pronunciation

      [edit]
       
      • (Brazil) IPA(key): /ˈnõ.mi/
      • (Brazil) IPA(key): /ˈnõ.mi/
        • (Southern Brazil) IPA(key): /ˈno.me/
      • (Portugal) IPA(key): /ˈno.mɨ/

      • (Rural Central Brazil) IPA(key): /ˈno.mʲ/
      • Audio (Portugal (Porto)):(file)
      • Rhymes: (Portugal) -omɨ, (Brazil) -õmi, (Southern Brazil) -ome
      • Hyphenation: no‧me

      Noun

      [edit]

      nome m (plural nomes)

      1. name (word or phrase which identifies an individual person, place, class, or thing)
        • 2000, J. K. Rowling, translated by Lia Wyler, Harry Potter e a Câmara Secreta [Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets] (Harry Potter; 2), Rio de Janeiro: Rocco, →ISBN, page 264:
          [...] e as letras do seu nome se rearrumaram.
          [...] and the letters of his name rearranged themselves.
      2. name (what somebody is known for)
        Preciso limpar meu nome.
        I must clear my name.
      3. (grammar) noun
        1. (grammar, loosely) substantive or adjective
      4. insult (used in the expression chamar nomes)
